Frequency: compare with $\sin(kz - \omega t)$. This gives $\omega = 2\pi\times10^6\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$, so $f = 10^6\ \text{Hz}$.
Wavelength in the medium: $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{10^8}{10^6} = 100\ \text{m}$. The value 300 m is the free-space wavelength $c/f$, so statement (2) is incorrect.
Magnetic field direction: $\vec E$ is along $\hat x$ and propagation is along $+\hat z$. Since $\hat x \times \hat y = \hat z$, $\vec B$ must lie along $+\hat y$ and be in phase with $\vec E$.
Magnetic field magnitude: in the medium $B_0 = \dfrac{E_0}{v}$. So the correct relation is $B_y = \dfrac{E_0}{v}\sin(kz - 2\pi\times10^6 t)$.
The given form $B_y = \dfrac{B_0}{v}\sin(\ldots)$ divides a magnetic amplitude by a speed. Its unit is $\text{T s m}^{-1}$, which is not a magnetic field, so statement (3) is incorrect.
Direction of propagation: the phase $(kz - \omega t)$ stays constant only if $z$ increases with $t$, so the wave moves along $+z$. Statement (4) is correct.
Hence statements (2) and (3) are both incorrect, which is why NTA accepted both options.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): The wavelength of the electromagnetic wave inside the medium is 300 m; and Option (3): The magnetic field is given by the relation $B_y = \frac{B_0}{v}\sin(kz - 2\pi\times10^6 t)$ (both accepted)
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) is a correct statement because $v = c/\sqrt{9} = 10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Option (4) is correct because the phase $(kz - \omega t)$ describes a wave moving along $+z$. Neither can be the 'incorrect choice'.
solution.common_trap: Students calculate $\lambda = c/f = 300\ \text{m}$ using the vacuum speed, forgetting that the speed, and hence the wavelength, drop by a factor of $\sqrt{\epsilon_r} = 3$ inside the dielectric, while the frequency stays the same.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember that $\lambda_{\text{medium}} = \lambda_0/n$ with $n = \sqrt{\epsilon_r} = 3$, giving $300/3 = 100\ \text{m}$ instantly. A quick unit check ($B_0/v$ is not in tesla) rules out (3) without further work.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: First law of thermodynamics
questions.question: One mole of an ideal monatomic gas undergoes a cyclic process as shown in the figure. The total heat supplied to the gas is :
questions.diagram_description: p-V diagram with p in $N/m^2$ on vertical axis and V in $m^3$ on horizontal axis. A rectangular cycle a→b→c→d→a: a at (2, 300), b at (5, 300), c at (5, 100), d at (2, 100). Arrows: a to b rightwards along p=300, b to c downwards along V=5, c to d leftwards along p=100, d to a upwards along V=2 (clockwise cycle).

solution.key_concept: For a complete cycle $\Delta U = 0$, so by the first law the net heat supplied equals the net work done, which is the area enclosed by the cycle on the $p$-$V$ diagram.
steps: The gas returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = 0$. The first law $Q = \Delta U + W$ then gives $Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{net}}$.
The work done in the cycle equals the area of the rectangle $abcd$: $W = (V_b - V_a)(p_a - p_d)$.
Substituting the values: $W = (5 - 2)\,\text{m}^3 \times (300 - 100)\,\text{N/m}^2 = 3 \times 200 = 600\ \text{J}$.
The cycle runs clockwise ($a \to b \to c \to d$), so the net work is done by the gas and is positive: $W = +600\ \text{J}$.
Therefore the total (net) heat supplied is $Q = W = 600\ \text{J}$.
solution.why_not_others: 400 J and 500 J come from misreading the rectangle's sides. 800 J results from wrongly using $p = 300 + 100$ or similar. Only the enclosed area $3 \times 200 = 600$ J is the net heat.
solution.common_trap: Students often add only the heat absorbed in the steps $d \to a$ and $a \to b$, which gives $600 + 2250 = 2850$ J, instead of the net heat over the cycle, or they treat the cycle as anticlockwise and change the sign.
solution.time_saving_tip: For any closed cycle, the net heat equals the enclosed area on the $p$-$V$ graph. Just multiply the rectangle's sides ($\Delta V \times \Delta p$), and the 'monatomic' detail is not needed.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Bohr model and energy levels
questions.question: Consider that an electron is revolving in an excited state of Hydrogen atom with velocity $\sqrt{25.6}\times10^{5}\ ms^{-1}$. The radius of the orbit is $x\times10^{-9}$ m. The value of $x$ is : (Take the mass of electron to be $9\times10^{-31}$ kg, charge of electron $= -1.6\times10^{-19}$ C and $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9\times10^{9}\ N\,m^2\,C^{-2}$]

solution.key_concept: In the Bohr model, the Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force, $\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{e^2}{r^2}$, which gives $r=\frac{ke^2}{mv^2}$.
steps: Equate the electrostatic force to the centripetal force for hydrogen ($Z=1$): $\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{ke^2}{r^2}$. This gives $r=\frac{ke^2}{mv^2}$.
Numerator: $ke^2=9\times10^{9}\times(1.6\times10^{-19})^2=9\times10^{9}\times2.56\times10^{-38}=2.304\times10^{-28}$ $\text{N m}^2$.
Denominator: $v^2=25.6\times10^{10}\ \text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}$, so $mv^2=9\times10^{-31}\times25.6\times10^{10}=2.304\times10^{-19}$ $\text{J}$.
Compare with $r=x\times10^{-9}$ m to get $x=1$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (3), $x=2$, results from forgetting to square $v$ properly or from mishandling a factor of 2. Options (1) and (2) come from errors in the powers of ten or from using $r\propto n^2$ with a guessed $n$.
solution.common_trap: Students substitute $v=25.6\times10^{5}$ instead of $\sqrt{25.6}\times10^{5}$, or square the factor $25.6$ again, which wrecks the powers of ten.
solution.time_saving_tip: Notice that $9\times2.56=2.304$ appears in both the numerator ($ke^2$) and the denominator ($mv^2$). The mantissas cancel, so only the powers of ten remain: $10^{-28}/10^{-19}=10^{-9}$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Vehicle on a level circular road and on a banked road
questions.question: A car travels on a circular racetrack of radius 50 m, which is banked at an angle $\theta$. If the car travels at a speed $10\ ms^{-1}$, then the wear and tear on its tyres is minimum. Taking the acceleration due to gravity to be $10\ ms^{-2}$, the value of $\theta$ is:

solution.key_concept: Tyre wear is minimum when no friction is needed, which happens at the optimum banking speed $v_0$ where $\tan\theta = \frac{v_0^2}{rg}$.
steps: Minimum wear and tear means friction between the tyres and the road is not needed. The car moves at the optimum speed $v_0$ for that banking.
Without friction, only the normal force $N$ and gravity $mg$ act on the car.
Vertical balance: $N\cos\theta = mg$.
Horizontal component supplies the centripetal force: $N\sin\theta = \frac{mv_0^2}{r}$.
Dividing the two equations: $\tan\theta = \frac{v_0^2}{rg}$.
Substituting values: $\tan\theta = \frac{(10)^2}{50 \times 10} = \frac{100}{500} = \frac{1}{5}$.
Therefore $\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (2), $\tan^{-1}(2/5)$, comes from wrongly using $\frac{2v^2}{rg}$, or from taking $r = 25$ m. Options (3) and (4) contain $\sqrt{3}$, which cannot come from $\frac{v^2}{rg}$ with these values.
solution.common_trap: Students often bring in a friction coefficient or use the maximum-speed formula, missing that 'minimum wear and tear' simply means zero friction.
solution.time_saving_tip: Read 'minimum wear and tear' as 'no friction' and directly compute $\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg} = \frac{100}{500}$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Semiconductor diode: I-V characteristics in forward and reverse bias
questions.question: Three identical p-n junction diodes $D_1, D_2$ and $D_3$ are connected across a battery as shown in the figure. If the width of the depletion regions of $D_1, D_2$ and $D_3$ are $W_1, W_2$ and $W_3$, respectively, then the correct option is:
questions.diagram_description: Three parallel branches connected between a left node and a right node, across a 5V battery at the bottom. Top branch: 1kΩ resistor in series with diode $D_1$ pointing right (forward from left to right). Middle branch: 1kΩ resistor in series with diode $D_2$ pointing right, but the branch has an open gap (break) after $D_2$ before the right node. Bottom branch: diode $D_3$ pointing left (reversed) in series with 1kΩ resistor. Battery of 5V connects the left and right nodes.

solution.key_concept: Depletion width depends on bias: it narrows under forward bias, keeps its equilibrium value at zero bias, and widens under reverse bias, so $W_{reverse} > W_{unbiased} > W_{forward}$.
steps: All three branches are in parallel across the same $5\,V$ battery, which drives the left node to the higher potential (this polarity is the one consistent with the key). Read each diode's arrow relative to that node.

$D_1$ (top branch): its arrow points from the left node to the right node. The p-side is at higher potential, so $D_1$ is forward biased. The barrier is lowered and its depletion region narrows, giving the smallest $W_1$.

$D_2$ (middle branch): the branch is broken by an open gap, so no current flows ($I = 0$). With no current there is no drop across the $1\,k\Omega$ resistor, and the whole $5\,V$ appears across the gap, not the diode. $D_2$ is therefore effectively unbiased and keeps its equilibrium width $W_2 = W_0$.

$D_3$ (bottom branch): its arrow points from right to left, opposite to $D_1$. The n-side is at higher potential, so $D_3$ is reverse biased. The barrier rises and its depletion region widens, giving the largest $W_3$.
Comparing the three: $W_{reverse} > W_{zero\,bias} > W_{forward}$, so $W_3 > W_2 > W_1$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) reverses the whole order. Options (2) and (4) wrongly make a forward-biased and a reverse-biased diode equal in width, or treat the open-circuit diode $D_2$ as if it were biased.
solution.common_trap: Assuming $D_2$ gets the full $5\,V$ because it is connected to the battery, when the open gap means it carries no current and sits at zero bias.
solution.time_saving_tip: Classify each diode as forward, open/zero or reverse, then apply forward < zero < reverse for depletion width; only option (3) matches.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Applications of electromagnetic waves
questions.question: The following table presents the part of the electromagnetic spectrum and their corresponding major applications. The correct option is :

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: For AM and FM communication systems

solution.key_concept: Each region of the electromagnetic spectrum has a characteristic use set by its frequency and energy: microwaves heat food, UV kills microbes, gamma rays destroy cancer cells and radio waves carry AM/FM signals.
steps: P (Microwave): The frequency of microwaves ($\sim 2.45\,\text{GHz}$ in ovens) makes water molecules in food oscillate, and this produces heat. So P → II (warming the food).
Q (UV rays): UV photons are energetic enough to damage the DNA of bacteria and viruses, so UV lamps are used to sterilise and purify water. So Q → I (purifying water).
R (Gamma rays): Gamma rays have the highest energy (shortest $\lambda$, below about $10^{-12}\,\text{m}$). They are used in radiotherapy to kill cancer cells. So R → IV (treating cancer cells).
S (Radio waves): AM uses about $530\,\text{kHz}$–$1710\,\text{kHz}$ and FM uses about $88$–$108\,\text{MHz}$, both in the radio band. So S → III (AM and FM communication).
The correct matching is P-II, Q-I, R-IV, S-III, which is option (3).
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (2) pair microwaves with water purification, but microwaves heat matter rather than sterilise it. Option (4) gives cancer treatment to UV and water purification to radio waves, but radio photons carry far too little energy to kill microbes.
solution.common_trap: Students often mix up UV and gamma rays because both are 'harmful/medical' radiations. UV is for sterilisation and water purification, while gamma rays, being far more penetrating, are for cancer therapy.
solution.time_saving_tip: Fix the most certain pair first: microwave → warming food (P-II). Only options (3) and (4) survive. Then radio → AM/FM (S-III) leaves only option (3).

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Elastic and inelastic collisions in one and two dimensions
questions.question: Bob B of mass $m$ at rest is hanging vertically from the ceiling via a massless string of length 10 m, as shown in the figure. Point mass A of mass $m$ travelling horizontally with speed $10\ ms^{-1}$ hits bob B elastically. The bob B rises $h$ meter after the collision. Taking the acceleration due to gravity $g = 10\ ms^{-2}$ and neglecting the size of the bob, the value of $h$ is :
questions.diagram_description: A vertical string hanging from a horizontal ceiling with bob B at its lower end. Point mass A to the left of B moving horizontally towards B with speed $10\ ms^{-1}$ (dashed arrow pointing right).

solution.key_concept: In a 1-D elastic collision between equal masses with one at rest, the velocities are exchanged, and the struck bob converts its kinetic energy into height: $h = \frac{v^2}{2g}$.
steps: Masses are equal ($m_A = m_B = m$) and B is initially at rest, so in a head-on elastic collision the velocities are exchanged.
After the collision $v_A = 0$ and $v_B = 10\ ms^{-1}$, horizontally.
Tension in the string is always perpendicular to B's velocity, so it does no work and mechanical energy of B is conserved: $\frac{1}{2}mv_B^2 = mgh$.
Substituting: $h = \frac{v_B^2}{2g} = \frac{(10)^2}{2 \times 10} = 5\ m$.
Check: $h = 5\ m < L = 10\ m$, so B swings up only to below the horizontal level of the support. The string stays taut and B momentarily comes to rest at that height. Hence $h = 5\ m$.
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) 8 and (2) 7 would need B to leave with more than $10\ ms^{-1}$, which is impossible since A's entire velocity is only transferred, never amplified. Option (4) 2.5 comes from wrongly halving the energy, e.g. using $\frac{v^2}{4g}$ or assuming B gets only part of A's kinetic energy.
solution.common_trap: Students often treat the collision as perfectly inelastic or share the kinetic energy between A and B, giving a smaller $h$ instead of using full velocity exchange.
solution.time_saving_tip: Equal masses with an elastic collision means B leaves with $10\ ms^{-1}$, so directly write $h = \frac{v^2}{2g} = 5\ m$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Law of equipartition of energy and specific heat capacities of gases
questions.question: An ideal gas is made of polyatomic molecules. Each of the molecules has three translational, three rotational and $f$ number of vibrational modes. If the ratio of heat capacities $\frac{C_p}{C_v}$ of the gas is $\frac{8}{7}$, then the value of $f$ is:

solution.key_concept: By equipartition, $C_v = \frac{F}{2}R$ and $\gamma = 1 + \frac{2}{F}$, where each vibrational mode contributes 2 to $F$ (kinetic and potential energy) while each translational or rotational mode contributes 1.
steps: Count the effective degrees of freedom. Translational modes give $3$ and rotational modes give $3$. Each of the $f$ vibrational modes gives $2$ quadratic terms ($\frac{1}{2}kT$ for kinetic energy plus $\frac{1}{2}kT$ for potential energy). So $F = 3 + 3 + 2f = 6 + 2f$.
Energy per mole: $U = \frac{F}{2}RT$, so $C_v = \frac{F}{2}R$ and $C_p = C_v + R = \left(\frac{F}{2}+1\right)R$.
Therefore $\gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v} = 1 + \frac{2}{F}$.
Substitute $\gamma = \frac{8}{7}$: $1 + \frac{2}{F} = \frac{8}{7} \Rightarrow \frac{2}{F} = \frac{1}{7} \Rightarrow F = 14$.
Solve for $f$: $6 + 2f = 14 \Rightarrow f = 4$.
solution.why_not_others: Options (2), (3) and (4) give $F = 12, 10, 8$, i.e. $\gamma = \frac{7}{6}, \frac{6}{5}, \frac{5}{4}$, none of which equals $\frac{8}{7}$.
solution.common_trap: Counting each vibrational mode as only one degree of freedom gives $6 + f = 14$, so $f = 8$ (not among the options); each vibrational mode actually carries $kT$ of energy, counting as 2.
solution.time_saving_tip: Use $\gamma = 1 + \frac{2}{F}$ directly: $\gamma - 1 = \frac{1}{7}$ gives $F = 14$ at once, then $f = \frac{14 - 6}{2} = 4$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Aldol condensation, Cannizzaro reaction and haloform reaction
questions.question: For the following reaction sequence, choose the correct option.
options: If P is the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid, Q is a primary alcohol.
P and Q are aromatic compounds.
If P gives a carboxylic acid on acidification, Q gives a poisonous gas on exposure to air and light.
Both P and Q are carbonyl compounds.
questions.diagram_description: Benzene ring reacting with reagents (i) $CH_3COCl, AlCl_3$ and (ii) $NaOCl$ written over a reaction arrow, giving products P + Q.

solution.key_concept: Friedel–Crafts acylation converts benzene to acetophenone, a methyl ketone, which undergoes the haloform reaction with $NaOCl$ to give sodium benzoate and chloroform.
steps: Step (i), Friedel–Crafts acylation: $C_6H_6 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{AlCl_3} C_6H_5COCH_3 + HCl$. The product is acetophenone, a methyl ketone.

Step (ii), haloform reaction: a $CH_3CO-$ group reacts with $NaOCl$. It gives the sodium salt of the acid with one carbon less, plus haloform: $C_6H_5COCH_3 + 3NaOCl \rightarrow C_6H_5COCCl_3 + 3NaOH$, then $C_6H_5COCCl_3 + NaOH \rightarrow C_6H_5COONa + CHCl_3$.
So $P = C_6H_5COONa$ (sodium benzoate) and $Q = CHCl_3$ (chloroform).
Statement (1): $P$ is indeed a carboxylate salt, but $Q$ is $CHCl_3$, not a primary alcohol. False.
Statement (2): $P$ is aromatic, but $CHCl_3$ is not. False.

Statement (3): $P$ gives benzoic acid on acidification, $C_6H_5COONa + HCl \rightarrow C_6H_5COOH + NaCl$. $Q$ is slowly oxidised by air in light to poisonous phosgene: $2CHCl_3 + O_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2COCl_2 + 2HCl$. True.
Statement (4): neither sodium benzoate nor chloroform is an aldehyde or ketone. False.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): If P gives a carboxylic acid on acidification, Q gives a poisonous gas on exposure to air and light.
solution.why_not_others: Options (1), (2) and (4) all fail because $Q$ is chloroform. It is not an alcohol, not aromatic and not a carbonyl compound, so only $P$ fits the first part of those statements.
solution.common_trap: Students confuse the haloform reaction with the Cannizzaro reaction. They then assume an alcohol plus a carboxylate salt form, but acetophenone has α-hydrogens and gives $CHCl_3$, not an alcohol.
solution.time_saving_tip: Spot the pattern 'methyl ketone + $NaOX$', which always gives $RCOONa + CHX_3$. Then recall that chloroform forms phosgene in air and light, which is why it is stored in dark bottles filled to the brim.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Isomerism in coordination compounds
questions.question: Given below are two statements: (Given : $oxH_2 = HOOC-COOH$) In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct.

solution.key_concept: An octahedral complex is chiral (optically active) only if it has no plane or centre of symmetry; complexes of type $[M(AA)_3]$ and cis-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$ are chiral, while trans-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$ is not.
steps: Oxalate, $ox^{2-}$ ($C_2O_4^{2-}$), is a symmetrical bidentate ligand (AA type).

Statement I: $[Fe(ox)_3]^{3-}$ is of the type $[M(AA)_3]$. The three chelate rings wrap around the metal like a propeller, giving $\Delta$ and $\Lambda$ forms. These are non-superimposable mirror images.
$[M(AA)_3]$ has no plane of symmetry and no centre of symmetry, so it is chiral. Statement I is correct.
Statement II: trans-$[Cr(H_2O)_2(ox)_2]^-$ is of the type trans-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$. The two $H_2O$ ligands sit on the axis, and both oxalate rings lie in the equatorial plane.
That equatorial plane is a mirror plane, and the complex also has a centre of symmetry. So its mirror image is superimposable and the complex is achiral. Statement II is incorrect.
(Only the cis isomer of $[Cr(H_2O)_2(ox)_2]^-$ is optically active.)
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect.
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (4) would require the trans isomer to be chiral, but its equatorial mirror plane rules this out. Option (2) wrongly denies the well-known $\Delta/\Lambda$ optical isomerism of $[M(AA)_3]$ complexes.
solution.common_trap: Students often assume any complex containing chelating ligands is optically active, forgetting that the trans-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$ arrangement has a plane of symmetry.
solution.time_saving_tip: Memorise the rule: $[M(AA)_3]$ and cis-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$ are chiral; trans-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$ is never chiral.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Inductive effect, electromeric effect, resonance and hyperconjugation
questions.question: The following carbocation is stabilized by the interaction of the empty $p$ orbital with
questions.diagram_description: Structure of 1-phenylethyl carbocation: a benzene ring attached to a carbon bearing a positive charge (⊕), which is also bonded to a $CH_3$ group ($C_6H_5-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_3$).

solution.key_concept: A carbocation's empty $p$ orbital is stabilized only by donation of electron density from adjacent filled orbitals: filled $\pi$ orbitals (resonance) and filled $\sigma_{C-H}$ orbitals (hyperconjugation).
steps: Identify the species: $C_6H_5-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_3$ is a secondary benzylic carbocation. Its cationic carbon is $sp^2$ hybridised and carries a vacant $2p$ orbital.

An empty orbital is stabilized only when a neighbouring orbital donates electron density into it. Interaction with another empty orbital ($\sigma^*$ or $\pi^*$) transfers no electrons, so it gives no stabilization.

Resonance: the vacant $p$ orbital overlaps with the filled $\pi$ orbitals of the benzene ring. This delocalises the positive charge onto the ortho and para positions. This is a filled $\pi \rightarrow$ empty $p$ interaction.

Hyperconjugation: the $CH_3$ group has three $\alpha$-$C-H$ bonds. Their filled $\sigma_{C-H}$ orbitals overlap with the empty $p$ orbital, giving 3 hyperconjugative structures. This is a filled $\sigma \rightarrow$ empty $p$ interaction.
So the carbocation is stabilized by filled $\sigma$ and filled $\pi$ orbitals, which is option (1).
solution.why_not_others: Options (2), (3) and (4) all include an empty orbital ($\sigma$, $\sigma^*$ or $\pi^*$). An empty orbital has no electrons to donate to the vacant $p$ orbital, so it cannot stabilize the cation. Option (3) is also wrong because it pairs empty $\sigma^*$ with filled $\pi$; the $\sigma^*$ interaction applies to carbanions or negative hyperconjugation, not to carbocations.
solution.common_trap: Students recall '$\sigma \rightarrow \sigma^*$' or '$\pi^*$' from hyperconjugation and back-bonding discussions and wrongly pick an option containing antibonding orbitals, forgetting that a cation needs an electron donor.
solution.time_saving_tip: Empty orbital needs electrons, so the stabilizing orbitals must be filled. Only option (1) contains filled orbitals alone, so you can mark it immediately.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of inorganic compounds: Mohr's salt and potash alum
questions.question: In potash alum, the ratio of $K^+$ and $SO_4^{2-}$ ions is

solution.key_concept: Potash alum is the double salt $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot 24H_2O$, i.e. $KAl(SO_4)_2\cdot 12H_2O$, so ion ratios come straight from its formula.
steps: Write the formula of potash alum: $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot 24H_2O$.
Count the ions in this formula: $K^+ = 2$, $Al^{3+} = 2$ and $SO_4^{2-} = 1 + 3 = 4$.
Check with the simplest formula $KAl(SO_4)_2\cdot 12H_2O$: it has 1 $K^+$ and 2 $SO_4^{2-}$, giving $1:2$.
Check charge balance: $(+1) + (+3) + 2(-2) = 0$, so the formula is consistent.
solution.why_not_others: $2:1$ inverts the ratio. $2:3$ and $3:2$ come from counting the sulphates of only $K_2SO_4$ or only $Al_2(SO_4)_3$ instead of adding both $(1 + 3 = 4)$.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting to add the sulphate from $K_2SO_4$ to the three sulphates from $Al_2(SO_4)_3$, or reading the ratio in reverse order.
solution.time_saving_tip: Memorise alum as $KAl(SO_4)_2\cdot 12H_2O$. The ratio $K^+ : Al^{3+} : SO_4^{2-} = 1:1:2$ can then be read off directly.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Protein structure: primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary
questions.question: The correct statement about peptides and proteins is
options: Tertiary structure of proteins has two or more polypeptide subunits.
Only the proteins having a quaternary structure are biologically active.
In $\beta$-pleated sheet structures, peptide chains are held together by intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
In $\alpha$-helices, the polypeptide chain is twisted into a left-handed screw (helix) through intramolecular hydrogen bonds.

solution.key_concept: The four levels of protein structure differ in what they describe and in the bonds that stabilise them: H-bonds within one chain in the $\alpha$-helix, H-bonds between chains in the $\beta$-pleated sheet, and subunit association only in quaternary structure.
steps: Statement (1): Tertiary structure is the overall 3-D folding of a single polypeptide chain. An arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits is quaternary structure, so (1) is false.
Statement (2): Many single-chain proteins are fully biologically active with only a tertiary structure, e.g. myoglobin and many enzymes. Quaternary structure is not required, so (2) is false.

Statement (3): In a $\beta$-pleated sheet, the peptide chains lie side by side almost fully extended. Neighbouring chains are joined by H-bonds between $\ce{C=O}$ of one chain and $\ce{N-H}$ of the adjacent chain. These are intermolecular (inter-chain) H-bonds, so (3) is true.

Statement (4): The $\alpha$-helix is a right-handed helix. It is stabilised by intramolecular H-bonds between the $\ce{C=O}$ of residue $n$ and the $\ce{N-H}$ of residue $n+4$. The word 'left-handed' makes (4) false.
Only statement (3) is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): In $\beta$-pleated sheet structures, peptide chains are held together by intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
solution.why_not_others: Option (4) uses the correct bond type (intramolecular H-bonds) but the wrong handedness; the $\alpha$-helix is right-handed. Option (1) describes quaternary structure, not tertiary, and option (2) is wrong because single-chain proteins can be biologically active.
solution.common_trap: Students see 'intramolecular hydrogen bonds' in option (4), recognise it as correct for the $\alpha$-helix, and miss that 'left-handed' should be right-handed.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember the pair '$\alpha$-helix = right-handed, intra-chain H-bonds; $\beta$-sheet = inter-chain H-bonds'. Statement (3) then matches immediately and the others can be eliminated quickly.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Matter and its nature
questions.question: The numbers 17.0145 and 21.0235 were rounded to three figures after the decimal point. The resulting numbers, respectively, are

solution.key_concept: When the digit to be dropped is exactly $5$, the preceding digit stays the same if it is even and goes up by $1$ if it is odd (round-half-to-even rule).
steps: We keep three digits after the decimal point, so in each number the fourth decimal digit is dropped. In both numbers that digit is $5$.

Rule: if the dropped digit is greater than $5$, increase the preceding digit by $1$. If it is less than $5$, leave the preceding digit unchanged. If it is exactly $5$, leave the preceding digit unchanged when it is even and increase it by $1$ when it is odd.
For $17.0145$: the digit before the $5$ is $4$, which is even, so it stays. Result: $17.0145 \rightarrow 17.014$.
For $21.0235$: the digit before the $5$ is $3$, which is odd, so it becomes $4$. Result: $21.0235 \rightarrow 21.024$.
The rounded numbers are $17.014$ and $21.024$, which is option (3).
solution.why_not_others: Option (4) comes from always rounding a $5$ upward, which ignores the even/odd rule for $17.0145$. Options (1) and (2) mishandle $21.0235$: its preceding digit $3$ is odd, so it must be raised to $4$.
solution.common_trap: Applying the everyday 'always round $5$ up' habit, which gives $17.015$ and $21.024$ (option 4) instead of using the even/odd rule for a dropped $5$.
solution.time_saving_tip: When the dropped digit is $5$, just check whether the digit before it is even (keep it) or odd (add $1$). Here $4 \rightarrow 4$ and $3 \rightarrow 4$, so pick option (3) directly.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Solubility and solubility product
questions.question: The correct order of solubility of the given salts in water at 298 K is
questions.diagram_description: Table with columns 'Salt' and '$K_{sp}$ at 298 K': $AgBr$ — $5.0\times10^{-13}$; $Zn(OH)_2$ — $1.0\times10^{-15}$; $Hg_2Cl_2$ — $1.3\times10^{-18}$.

solution.key_concept: Solubility cannot be ranked from $K_{sp}$ alone when salts have different ion stoichiometry; convert each $K_{sp}$ to molar solubility $s$ ($K_{sp}=s^2$ for AB and $K_{sp}=4s^3$ for AB$_2$) and then compare $s$.
steps: $AgBr \rightleftharpoons Ag^+ + Br^-$ is an AB type salt, so $K_{sp}=s^2$. This gives $s=\sqrt{5.0\times10^{-13}}\approx 7.07\times10^{-7}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

$Zn(OH)_2 \rightleftharpoons Zn^{2+} + 2OH^-$ is an AB$_2$ type salt, so $K_{sp}=s(2s)^2=4s^3$. This gives $s^3=\dfrac{1.0\times10^{-15}}{4}=2.5\times10^{-16}$, so $s\approx 6.3\times10^{-6}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

Mercury(I) exists as the dimer $Hg_2^{2+}$, so $Hg_2Cl_2 \rightleftharpoons Hg_2^{2+} + 2Cl^-$ and $K_{sp}=4s^3$. This gives $s^3=\dfrac{1.3\times10^{-18}}{4}=3.25\times10^{-19}$, so $s\approx 6.9\times10^{-7}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.
Compare the molar solubilities: $6.3\times10^{-6}\,(Zn(OH)_2) > 7.07\times10^{-7}\,(AgBr) > 6.9\times10^{-7}\,(Hg_2Cl_2)$.
So the order of solubility is $Zn(OH)_2 > AgBr > Hg_2Cl_2$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) follows the raw $K_{sp}$ values, but $Zn(OH)_2$ is an AB$_2$ salt, so its solubility ($\sim10^{-6}$ M) exceeds that of $AgBr$ ($\sim10^{-7}$ M). Options (1) and (3) wrongly put $Hg_2Cl_2$ on top, although it has the lowest molar solubility.
solution.common_trap: Students either rank the salts directly by $K_{sp}$, or write mercurous chloride as $2Hg^+ + 2Cl^-$ instead of $Hg_2^{2+} + 2Cl^-$, which gives a wrong, much larger solubility.
solution.time_saving_tip: Estimate $s\approx\sqrt[3]{K_{sp}/4}$ only for the AB$_2$ salts. $Zn(OH)_2$ comes out near $6\times10^{-6}$, clearly the highest, which already eliminates options (1), (2) and (3).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Electron gain enthalpy
questions.question: Among the following options, the correct trend in the electron gain enthalpy is

solution.key_concept: Electron gain enthalpy grows more negative as atomic size decreases down to Cl, but F is anomalous: its very small 2p shell causes strong electron–electron repulsion, so Cl releases the most energy among the halogens.
steps: The question compares the magnitude of negative electron gain enthalpy, i.e. how much energy is released when $X(g) + e^- \rightarrow X^-(g)$.
Approximate values ($\Delta_{eg}H$ in kJ mol$^{-1}$): $F = -328$, $Cl = -349$, $Br = -325$, $I = -295$.
Down the group from Cl to I, atomic size increases. The incoming electron is held less firmly by the nucleus, so less energy is released: $Cl > Br > I$.
F is the exception. Its compact $2p$ subshell is already crowded, so the added electron feels strong interelectronic repulsion. This makes $|\Delta_{eg}H|$ of F smaller than that of Cl.
Br ($-325$) is only slightly less negative than F ($-328$), so F still sits above Br.
Combining these gives the order $Cl > F > Br > I$ (by magnitude of energy released).
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) applies the simple size trend and ignores fluorine's electron–electron repulsion anomaly. Options (2) and (4) wrongly place the larger Br or I above Cl.
solution.common_trap: Assuming fluorine, being the most electronegative element, must also have the most negative electron gain enthalpy.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember the rule 'Cl has the highest electron gain enthalpy in the periodic table'. Only option (3) starts with Cl.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Ideal and non-ideal solutions
questions.question: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.

statements.A: For an ideal solution formed by mixing liquids P and Q, $\Delta_{mix}H = 0$ and $\Delta_{mix}V = 0$
statements.R: No interactions occur between P and Q

options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct

solution.key_concept: An ideal solution is one in which the P–Q interactions are nearly equal to the P–P and Q–Q interactions, so $\Delta_{mix}H = 0$ and $\Delta_{mix}V = 0$; it is not a case where interactions are absent.
steps: Assertion: an ideal solution obeys Raoult's law over the whole concentration range. For such a solution, no heat is absorbed or released on mixing ($\Delta_{mix}H = 0$), and the volume of the solution equals the sum of the component volumes ($\Delta_{mix}V = 0$). So A is correct.
Reason: R says no interactions occur between P and Q. This is false. P and Q molecules do attract each other in an ideal solution.

The real condition for ideality is that the $P\text{–}Q$ attractive forces are nearly equal to the $P\text{–}P$ and $Q\text{–}Q$ forces. Bonds broken and bonds formed on mixing then balance, which gives $\Delta_{mix}H = 0$.
If there were truly no interactions between P and Q, the attractions broken on mixing would not be compensated. The solution would then show large positive deviations, so it would not be ideal.
Conclusion: A is correct but R is not correct. This matches option (3) and agrees with the official answer.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is correct but R is not correct
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (2) both require R to be true, but interactions do exist in an ideal solution; they are only equal in strength. Option (4) fails because A is a standard, correct property of ideal solutions.
solution.common_trap: Students confuse 'equal interactions' with 'no interactions', or mix up the ideal-solution idea with the 'no intermolecular forces' assumption for ideal gases, and so wrongly accept R.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember: ideal solution means $A\text{–}B \approx A\text{–}A \approx B\text{–}B$. Any statement claiming 'no interaction' is false, so options (1) and (2) go immediately.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative analysis: detection of nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens
questions.question: The amino acid that gives a red-blood colour on treating its sodium fusion extract with sodium nitroprusside is

solution.key_concept: Only an organic compound containing sulphur gives a positive sulphur test on its sodium fusion extract (Lassaigne's extract), so the answer must be the sulphur-containing amino acid.
steps: During sodium fusion, sulphur in the compound becomes sodium sulphide: $2Na + S \rightarrow Na_2S$.
If nitrogen is also present, sodium thiocyanate forms as well: $Na + C + N + S \rightarrow NaSCN$.
With sodium nitroprusside, sulphide gives a violet/purple complex: $S^{2-} + [Fe(CN)_5NO]^{2-} \rightarrow [Fe(CN)_5NOS]^{4-}$.
With $FeCl_3$, thiocyanate gives the blood-red colour: $Fe^{3+} + SCN^- \rightarrow [Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$.
Whichever of these colours is meant, the compound must contain sulphur.
Leucine ($C_6H_{13}NO_2$), threonine ($C_4H_9NO_3$) and serine ($C_3H_7NO_3$) contain no sulphur.
Methionine, $CH_3SCH_2CH_2CH(NH_2)COOH$, contains sulphur (and nitrogen), so it is the answer.
solution.why_not_others: Threonine and serine carry $-OH$ groups and leucine is a plain alkyl amino acid. None of them contains sulphur, so their extracts give no sulphur test.
solution.common_trap: Students mix up the colour–reagent pairs: nitroprusside with $S^{2-}$ gives violet, while blood-red comes from $Fe^{3+}$ with $SCN^-$ (both N and S present).
solution.time_saving_tip: Any sulphur-test question on amino acids reduces to spotting the sulphur-containing one, either methionine or cysteine.
solution.key_check_note: The question pairs the wrong colour with the reagent. Nitroprusside gives a violet colour with sulphide; blood-red is the $FeCl_3$/thiocyanate test. Both tests point only to methionine, so the key (3) stands.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Electrode potentials and standard electrode potential
questions.question: The standard electrode potential ($E^\circ$) for the half-cell reaction $Fe^{3+} + e^- \rightarrow Fe^{2+}$ at 298 K is (Given: $E^\circ(Fe^{3+}/Fe) = -0.04$ V and $E^\circ(Fe^{2+}/Fe) = -0.44$ V at 298 K)

solution.key_concept: Electrode potentials are intensive and cannot be added or subtracted directly; combine half-reactions through $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$, which is additive.
steps: Write the given couples: (i) $Fe^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Fe$, $E_1^\circ = -0.04$ V, $n_1 = 3$; (ii) $Fe^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Fe$, $E_2^\circ = -0.44$ V, $n_2 = 2$.
Target: $Fe^{3+} + e^- \rightarrow Fe^{2+}$ = (i) $-$ (ii), with $n = 1$.
$\Delta G^\circ = \Delta G_1^\circ - \Delta G_2^\circ = 0.12F - 0.88F = -0.76F$.
$E^\circ = -\dfrac{\Delta G^\circ}{nF} = -\dfrac{-0.76F}{1 \cdot F} = +0.76$ V.
solution.why_not_others: $+0.40$ V comes from directly subtracting potentials, $(-0.04) - (-0.44)$, while ignoring the number of electrons. $-0.48$ V comes from simply adding the potentials, and $+0.92$ V comes from mixing up the electron-weighting terms. None of these accounts correctly for $nE^\circ$.
solution.common_trap: Students subtract the two $E^\circ$ values directly and get $+0.40$ V, forgetting that only $nE^\circ$ (i.e. $\Delta G^\circ$) is additive.
solution.time_saving_tip: Use $n_3E_3^\circ = n_1E_1^\circ - n_2E_2^\circ$ directly: $1 \cdot E^\circ = 3(-0.04) - 2(-0.44) = 0.76$ V.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Oxalic acid vs KMnO4 and Mohr's salt vs KMnO4
questions.question: In an acidic medium, 10 mL of 0.25 M oxalic acid is titrated with $KMnO_4$ solution. If the volume of $KMnO_4$ solution required to reach end point is 10 mL, the strength of the $KMnO_4$ solution is

solution.key_concept: At the end point, milliequivalents of oxidant equal milliequivalents of reductant ($N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$ with $N = M \times n$-factor). In acidic medium, $KMnO_4$ has $n = 5$ and oxalic acid has $n = 2$.
steps: Find the n-factor of $KMnO_4$ in acidic medium: $MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O$. Mn goes from $+7$ to $+2$, so $n = 5$.
Find the n-factor of oxalic acid: $C_2O_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2CO_2 + 2e^-$. Each C goes from $+3$ to $+4$, and there are 2 C atoms, so $n = 2$.
Equate milliequivalents: $M_1 n_1 V_1 = M_2 n_2 V_2$.
Substitute: $0.25 \times 2 \times 10 = M \times 5 \times 10$, which gives $5 = 50M$.

Solve: $M = 0.10$ M. (Check with the balanced equation: $2MnO_4^- + 5C_2O_4^{2-} + 16H^+ \rightarrow 2Mn^{2+} + 10CO_2 + 8H_2O$. Moles of $KMnO_4$ = $\frac{2}{5} \times 2.5$ mmol = $1$ mmol, and $1$ mmol in $10$ mL is $0.10$ M.)
solution.why_not_others: 0.25 M comes from assuming a 1:1 mole ratio, which ignores the n-factors. 0.20 M and 0.15 M come from using wrong n-factors, such as $n = 3$ for $KMnO_4$, which applies only in neutral medium.
solution.common_trap: Writing $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$ directly, without multiplying by the n-factors (5 for $KMnO_4$ in acid, 2 for oxalic acid).
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember the fixed ratio: in acidic medium, 2 mol $KMnO_4$ react with 5 mol oxalic acid. With equal volumes, $M_{KMnO_4} = \frac{2}{5} \times 0.25 = 0.10$ M.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Basic ideas of crystal field theory
questions.question: According to crystal field theory, the correct order of ligands with respect to their decreasing order of field strength is

solution.key_concept: The spectrochemical series ranks ligands by the crystal field splitting ($\Delta$) they produce: $I^- < Br^- < Cl^- < F^- < OH^- < H_2O < NH_3 < en < CN^- < CO$.
steps: Recall the spectrochemical series in increasing field strength: $I^- < Br^- < SCN^- < Cl^- < F^- < OH^- < C_2O_4^{2-} < H_2O < NCS^- < en \approx NH_3 < CN^- < CO$.
Place $CO$ first. It is the strongest-field ligand because it is a $\sigma$-donor and also a strong $\pi$-acceptor (back-bonding into its $\pi^*$ orbitals), which gives a very large $\Delta$.
Place $NH_3$ above $H_2O$. Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so $NH_3$ is a better $\sigma$-donor and produces a larger $\Delta$.
Place $Cl^-$ last. It is a weak-field halide and a $\pi$-donor, which reduces $\Delta$.
The decreasing order is therefore $CO > NH_3 > H_2O > Cl^-$, which matches option (1).
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) wrongly puts $H_2O$ above $NH_3$. Options (3) and (4) reverse the series by placing the weak-field ligand $Cl^-$ first and the strongest ligand $CO$ last.
solution.common_trap: Students often place $H_2O$ above $NH_3$, or assume the negatively charged $Cl^-$ must be a stronger ligand, forgetting that $\pi$-acceptor ability matters and charge does not decide field strength.
solution.time_saving_tip: Since $CO$ is always the strongest ligand, options (3) and (4) drop out at once. Then just check that $NH_3 > H_2O$ to pick option (1).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Entropy of the universe and Gibbs energy as criteria for spontaneity
questions.question: Two moles of an ideal gas undergo free expansion from 10 L to 100 L at 300 K. The values of $\Delta S_{system}$ and $\Delta S_{surroundings}$ are (R is universal gas constant)

solution.key_concept: Entropy is a state function, so $\Delta S_{system}$ for free expansion is found along a reversible isothermal path, $\Delta S = nR\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$; the surroundings exchange no heat, so $\Delta S_{surroundings} = 0$.
steps: In free expansion the gas expands against vacuum, so $p_{ext} = 0$ and $w = 0$. For an ideal gas at constant $T$, $\Delta U = 0$, so $q = 0$.

Entropy is a state function. Compute $\Delta S_{system}$ along a reversible isothermal path between the same initial and final states: $\Delta S_{system} = nR\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1} = 2.303\,nR\log\frac{V_2}{V_1}$.
Substitute: $\Delta S_{system} = 2.303 \times 2 \times R \times \log\frac{100}{10} = 2.303 \times 2 \times R \times 1 = 4.606R$.
The surroundings exchange no heat with the system, since $q_{actual} = 0$. Hence $\Delta S_{surroundings} = \frac{-q_{actual}}{T} = 0$.
So $\Delta S_{total} = 4.606R > 0$, which is consistent with free expansion being a spontaneous, irreversible process.
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) is the result for a reversible isothermal expansion, where $\Delta S_{total} = 0$. Free expansion is irreversible, and the surroundings gain no heat. Options (1) and (3) wrongly take $\Delta S_{system} = 0$ just because $q = 0$, forgetting that entropy is a state function.
solution.common_trap: Using $q_{actual} = 0$ to write $\Delta S_{system} = q/T = 0$, when $\Delta S$ must be calculated with $q_{rev}$ along a reversible path.
solution.time_saving_tip: For free expansion, remember $\Delta S_{surr} = 0$ and $\Delta S_{sys} = 2.303\,nR\log\frac{V_2}{V_1}$. A tenfold volume increase gives $\Delta S_{sys} = 2.303\,nR$ directly.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Differential and integral forms of zero and first order reactions
questions.question: $2A \xrightarrow{k} B$ is a zero-order reaction, where $k = 1.0$ mol $L^{-1}$ $min^{-1}$. If the initial concentration of A is 2 M, then the time taken to complete 75% of the reaction will be

solution.key_concept: For a zero-order reaction $2A \rightarrow B$, the rate is $-\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[A]}{dt} = k$. So A is consumed at $2k$, and the integrated form is $[A]_0 - [A] = 2kt$.
steps: Write the rate law with the stoichiometric coefficient included: $\text{Rate} = -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[A]}{dt} = k$, so $-\frac{d[A]}{dt} = 2k$.
Integrate for zero order: $[A]_0 - [A]_t = 2kt$.
75% of A reacts, so the amount consumed is $0.75 \times 2 = 1.5$ M, which leaves $[A]_t = 0.5$ M.
Substitute: $2 - 0.5 = 2 \times 1.0 \times t \Rightarrow 1.5 = 2t$.
Solve: $t = 0.75$ min.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1), 1.5 min, comes from ignoring the factor 2 and using $[A]_0 - [A] = kt$. Options (3) and (4) are the times for 50% and 100% completion if that same factor is ignored.
solution.common_trap: Students write $[A]_0 - [A] = kt$ and forget that the rate constant is defined per the reaction rate, so A disappears at $2k$ because of its coefficient 2.
solution.time_saving_tip: For $nA \rightarrow$ products at zero order, use $t = \frac{\Delta[A]}{nk}$ directly: $t = \frac{1.5}{2 \times 1} = 0.75$ min.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Transition elements: introduction, electronic configuration, occurrence and characteristics
questions.question: Given below are two statements : One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

statements.A: Generally, 3d transition metals have high melting points.
statements.R: Involvement of 3d-electrons in addition to 4s-electrons in the interatomic metallic bonding.

options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are correct and R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is correct but R is not correct.
A is not correct but R is correct.

solution.key_concept: The high melting points of 3d transition metals come from strong metallic bonding: both $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons, especially unpaired $d$ electrons, take part in interatomic bonding.
steps: Judge Assertion A: 3d transition metals generally have high melting points, mostly above $1000^\circ\text{C}$ (e.g., $\text{Fe} \approx 1538^\circ\text{C}$, $\text{Cr} \approx 1907^\circ\text{C}$). Zn ($\approx 420^\circ\text{C}$) is the main exception, which is why the statement says 'generally'. A is correct.
Judge Reason R: in transition metals, the $3d$ electrons take part in metallic bonding along with the $4s$ electrons. This is a well-established fact, so R is correct.
Link R to A: more electrons in the 'electron sea' give stronger metallic bonds. More energy is then needed to break the lattice, so the melting point is higher.

Check with the trend: melting points rise to a maximum near $d^5$ (Cr, about one unpaired electron per orbital). They then fall as the $d$ electrons pair up and contribute less to bonding. Zn ($3d^{10}$) has no unpaired $d$ electrons, so its melting point is very low. This confirms that R explains A.
Both statements are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) is wrong because $d$-electron participation is exactly the reason metallic bonding is strong and melting points are high. Options (3) and (4) are wrong because both statements are factually correct.
solution.common_trap: Students see the exceptions (Zn, Mn) and either mark A as wrong or choose option (2), forgetting that 'generally' allows exceptions and that $d$-electron bonding directly explains the high melting points.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember the line 'more unpaired $d$ electrons → stronger metallic bonding → higher m.p.'. Any A–R pair linking high m.p. of transition metals to $d$-electron involvement is option (1).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Kohlrausch's law and its applications
questions.question: For a salt XY, which is a strong electrolyte, the plot of $\Lambda_m$ versus $\sqrt{c}$ has a slope of $-90.0$ S $cm^2$ $mol^{-3/2}$ $L^{1/2}$ at 298 K. At 0.01 M concentration of XY, the value of $\Lambda_m$ is 145.0 S $cm^2$ $mol^{-1}$. The limiting molar conductivity of $Y^-$ ion ($\lambda^o_{Y^-}$, in S $cm^2$ $mol^{-1}$) at 298 K will be (Given : $\lambda^o_{X^+} = 74.0$ S $cm^2$ $mol^{-1}$)

solution.key_concept: For a strong electrolyte, the Debye–Hückel–Onsager equation $\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^o - A\sqrt{c}$ gives $\Lambda_m^o$, and Kohlrausch's law $\Lambda_m^o = \lambda^o_{X^+} + \lambda^o_{Y^-}$ then gives the individual ionic conductivity.
steps: For a strong electrolyte, $\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^o - A\sqrt{c}$. A plot of $\Lambda_m$ vs $\sqrt{c}$ is a straight line with slope $-A$, so $A = 90.0$ S $cm^2$ $mol^{-3/2}$ $L^{1/2}$.
Substitute: $145.0 = \Lambda_m^o - (90.0)(0.1) = \Lambda_m^o - 9.0$.
By Kohlrausch's law, $\Lambda_m^o(XY) = \lambda^o_{X^+} + \lambda^o_{Y^-}$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (3) $90.0$ simply copies the magnitude of the slope. The other values arise from using $c$ instead of $\sqrt{c}$, or from subtracting $9.0$ instead of adding it, which gives $\Lambda_m^o$ less than $\Lambda_m$. That is impossible, since molar conductivity increases on dilution.
solution.common_trap: Students often put $c = 0.01$ instead of $\sqrt{c} = 0.1$ into the equation, or treat the negative slope wrongly so that $\Lambda_m^o$ comes out smaller than $\Lambda_m$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Use $\lambda^o_{Y^-} = \Lambda_m + |\text{slope}|\sqrt{c} - \lambda^o_{X^+} = 145 + 9 - 74 = 80$ in one line.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Chemical equations and stoichiometry
questions.question: The amount of carbon dioxide evolved upon complete combustion of 116 g of n-butane is (Given: atomic mass in amu H=1, C=12 and O = 16)

solution.key_concept: Mole-to-mole stoichiometry from a balanced combustion equation: each mole of $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}$ gives 4 moles of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (conservation of carbon atoms).
steps: Write the balanced equation: $2\,\mathrm{C_4H_{10}} + 13\,\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 8\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 10\,\mathrm{H_2O}$.
Find the molar mass of n-butane: $M(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}) = 4(12) + 10(1) = 58\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.
Find the moles of butane: $n = \dfrac{116}{58} = 2\ \mathrm{mol}$.
Apply the mole ratio $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}} : \mathrm{CO_2} = 1 : 4$. This gives $n(\mathrm{CO_2}) = 2 \times 4 = 8\ \mathrm{mol}$.
Find the mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$, using $M(\mathrm{CO_2}) = 44\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$: $m = 8 \times 44 = 352\ \mathrm{g}$.
solution.why_not_others: 176 g results from using the wrong ratio, for example 1 mol butane giving 4 mol $\mathrm{CO_2}$ while treating 116 g as only 1 mol, or halving the answer by misreading the coefficients 2 : 8. The values 322 g and 362 g do not correspond to any whole-number mole count of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ ($44n$), so they are distractors.
solution.common_trap: Reading the coefficients of the balanced equation (2 : 8) as a 1 : 8 ratio, or forgetting to convert grams to moles before applying the ratio.
solution.time_saving_tip: Skip balancing the full equation and use carbon conservation: each $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}$ gives 4 $\mathrm{CO_2}$. So the mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is $\frac{116}{58} \times 4 \times 44 = 352\ \mathrm{g}$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Effect of temperature; Arrhenius theory
questions.question: For an elementary chemical reaction, the Arrhenius plot is given below. If the energy of activation is 6.64 kJ $mol^{-1}$ and R = 8.3 J $K^{-1}$ $mol^{-1}$, the temperature at which the rate constant becomes $e^2$ $min^{-1}$, is:
questions.diagram_description: Arrhenius plot: y-axis ln k with marks 2, 4, 6, 8; x-axis 1/T. A straight line with negative slope starts on the y-axis at ln k = 6 and decreases downward to the right, ending near the x-axis.

solution.key_concept: In the Arrhenius plot, $\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$, so the y-intercept of $\ln k$ vs $1/T$ gives $\ln A$ and the slope is $-E_a/R$.
steps: Write the linear form of the Arrhenius equation: $\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{R}\cdot\dfrac{1}{T}$.
From the graph, the line meets the $\ln k$ axis at 6, so $\ln A = 6$.
For $k = e^2\ \text{min}^{-1}$, $\ln k = 2$. Substituting gives $2 = 6 - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$, so $\dfrac{E_a}{RT} = 4$.
Solve for $T$: $T = \dfrac{E_a}{4R} = \dfrac{6640}{4 \times 8.3} = \dfrac{6640}{33.2} = 200\ \text{K}$.
solution.why_not_others: $125$ K or $150$ K follow from using a wrong intercept or a wrong $\ln k$ difference (for example $E_a/RT = 6$ or $2$ instead of $4$). $250$ K results from arithmetic slips such as dividing by $3.2R$.
solution.common_trap: Students forget to convert $E_a$ from kJ to J ($6.64$ kJ $= 6640$ J), or they take $\ln k = e^2$ instead of $\ln k = 2$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Read $\ln A$ directly from the intercept. Then $T = E_a / [R(\ln A - \ln k)]$, which here is $6640/(8.3 \times 4) = 200$ K in one line.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Electronic concepts of oxidation and reduction
questions.question: Given below are two statements: In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

statements.I: Heating NaCl with concentrated $H_2SO_4$ and $MnO_2$ results in oxidation of Mn.
statements.II: Heating NaI with concentrated $H_2SO_4$ and $MnO_2$ results in reduction of Mn.

options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct.

solution.key_concept: With concentrated $H_2SO_4$, $MnO_2$ acts as an oxidising agent: it oxidises halide ions to halogens and is itself reduced from Mn(+4) to Mn(+2).
steps: Find the oxidation state of Mn in $MnO_2$: $x + 2(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +4$.
Statement I: $4NaCl + MnO_2 + 4H_2SO_4 \rightarrow MnCl_2 + 4NaHSO_4 + 2H_2O + Cl_2$. In this reaction $Cl^-$ (−1) is oxidised to $Cl_2$ (0).
In the same reaction Mn changes from +4 in $MnO_2$ to +2 in $MnCl_2$. A decrease in oxidation number is reduction, not oxidation, so Statement I is incorrect.
Statement II: $2NaI + MnO_2 + 3H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2NaHSO_4 + MnSO_4 + 2H_2O + I_2$. Here $I^-$ (−1) is oxidised to $I_2$ (0).
Mn again goes from +4 to +2, so Mn is reduced. Statement II is correct.
Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct, which is Option (4).
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct.
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (3) fail because Mn is reduced, not oxidised, in the $NaCl$ reaction. Option (2) fails because Mn is indeed reduced in the $NaI$ reaction. The identity of the halide does not change the role of $MnO_2$ as the oxidant.
solution.common_trap: Students see the 'oxidising' conditions (conc. $H_2SO_4$ + $MnO_2$) and assume Mn is oxidised, forgetting that the oxidising agent itself gets reduced.
solution.time_saving_tip: $MnO_2$ (Mn = +4) is the classic oxidant that ends up as $Mn^{2+}$ in both reactions. So Mn is reduced in both cases: I is false and II is true.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Colour and magnetic properties
questions.question: Among the species given below, the spin-only magnetic moment is highest for (Given : Atomic number of Ti = 22, Mn = 25, Fe = 26 and Co = 27)

solution.key_concept: Spin-only magnetic moment is $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons fixed by the metal's $d^n$ count and the ligand field strength.
steps: $[Mn(CN)_6]^{3-}$: $Mn^{3+}$ is $3d^4$. $CN^-$ is a strong-field ligand, so the complex is low spin, $t_{2g}^4 e_g^0$. This gives $n = 2$ and $\mu = \sqrt{2(4)} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$ BM.
$[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$: $Fe^{3+}$ is $3d^5$. $CN^-$ makes it low spin, $t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$. This gives $n = 1$ and $\mu = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73$ BM.
$[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$: $Co^{3+}$ is $3d^6$. $NH_3$ acts as a strong-field ligand towards $Co^{3+}$, so the complex is low spin, $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$. This gives $n = 0$ and $\mu = 0$ (diamagnetic).
$[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$: $Ti^{3+}$ is $3d^1$. Field strength does not matter for one electron, $t_{2g}^1$. This gives $n = 1$ and $\mu = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73$ BM.
Comparing the values: $2.83 > 1.73 = 1.73 > 0$. The highest moment belongs to $[Mn(CN)_6]^{3-}$.
solution.why_not_others: Low-spin $Fe^{3+}$ ($t_{2g}^5$) and $Ti^{3+}$ ($d^1$) each have only one unpaired electron. $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$ is low-spin $d^6$ with all electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic.
solution.common_trap: Students count unpaired electrons as if every complex were high spin. That gives $Fe^{3+}$ 5 unpaired electrons and makes option (2) look like the answer, ignoring that $CN^-$ forces pairing.
solution.time_saving_tip: For octahedral strong-field complexes, unpaired electrons are: $d^4 \to 2$, $d^5 \to 1$, $d^6 \to 0$. Any $d^1$ ion always has 1. So the only species with 2 unpaired electrons, $Mn^{3+}$, wins at once.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Lanthanoids: electronic configuration, oxidation states and lanthanoid contraction
questions.question: The lanthanide ion having four unpaired electrons is (Given: Atomic numbers of $Ce = 58$, $Nd = 60$, $Tb = 65$ and $Ho = 67$)

solution.key_concept: A $Ln^{3+}$ ion has the configuration $[Xe]4f^{n}$ with $n = Z - 57$, and its unpaired electrons follow from Hund's rule over the seven $4f$ orbitals.
steps: Forming $Ln^{3+}$ removes the two $6s$ electrons and one $4f$ or $5d$ electron. This leaves $[Xe]4f^{n}$, where $n = Z - 57$.
$Ce^{3+}$: $n = 58 - 57 = 1$, so $4f^{1}$ gives 1 unpaired electron.
$Nd^{3+}$: $n = 60 - 57 = 3$, so $4f^{3}$ gives 3 unpaired electrons.
$Tb^{3+}$: $n = 65 - 57 = 8$, so $4f^{8}$ has 7 singly filled orbitals and 1 paired, giving $7 - 1 = 6$ unpaired electrons.
$Ho^{3+}$: $n = 67 - 57 = 10$, so $4f^{10}$ has 7 singly filled orbitals and 3 paired, giving $7 - 3 = 4$ unpaired electrons.
Only $Ho^{3+}$ has 4 unpaired electrons.
solution.why_not_others: $Ce^{3+}$ ($4f^1$) has 1 and $Nd^{3+}$ ($4f^3$) has 3 unpaired electrons. $Tb^{3+}$ ($4f^8$) has 6, not 4, because only one electron pairs up after the half-filled $4f^7$.
solution.common_trap: Students often miscount the $f$ electrons, for example taking $Ho^{3+}$ as $4f^{11}$ by forgetting that three electrons are removed. Others count $4f^{8}$ as having 8 unpaired electrons, ignoring that there are only 7 $f$ orbitals.
solution.time_saving_tip: For $4f^{n}$, unpaired electrons $= n$ if $n \le 7$, and $= 14 - n$ if $n > 7$. For $Ho^{3+}$: $14 - 10 = 4$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: IUPAC nomenclature of mononuclear coordination compounds
questions.question: The formula of tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride is

solution.key_concept: In IUPAC naming, the name inside the coordination sphere (ligands in alphabetical order plus the metal with its oxidation state) fixes the complex ion's charge, and the counter ions are added to balance that charge.
steps: Read the ligands from the name: tetraammine = $4\,NH_3$ (neutral), aqua = $1\,H_2O$ (neutral), chlorido = $1\,Cl^-$ (charge $-1$).
The metal is cobalt(III), so $Co^{3+}$.
Charge on the complex ion: $x = +3 + 4(0) + 0 + (-1) = +2$, giving $[Co(NH_3)_4(H_2O)Cl]^{2+}$.
The counter ion is chloride ($Cl^-$). Two are needed to balance $+2$, so the formula is $[Co(NH_3)_4(H_2O)Cl]Cl_2$.
Check the coordination number: $4 + 1 + 1 = 6$, which is octahedral and typical for $Co^{3+}$. The formula is consistent.
solution.why_not_others: Option (3) has only one counter $Cl^-$, which would require cobalt(II). Options (1) and (2) put water outside the coordination sphere as water of crystallisation, but 'aqua' in the name means water is a coordinated ligand. Option (1) is also a neutral-looking $Co^{2+}$ species, and option (2) leaves out the coordinated chlorido.
solution.common_trap: Students balance the counter ions using only the metal's oxidation state ($+3$, giving $Cl_3$) and forget that the coordinated chlorido ligand already contributes $-1$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Count anionic ligands inside the sphere and subtract from the metal's oxidation state: $3 - 1 = 2$ counter $Cl^-$. Only option (4) matches.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: First law: work, heat, internal energy and enthalpy
questions.question: Consider the reversible processes for 1.0 mol of an ideal gas as shown in the figure. $w_1$, $w_2$, $w_3$ and $w_4$ represent work done (in calories) in the processes 1, 2, 3 and 4, respectively; $\Delta U_2$ and $\Delta U_4$ are changes in the internal energy for the processes 2 and 4, respectively. [use $R = 2\ cal\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$] The correct option is
questions.diagram_description: Pressure (y-axis) vs Volume (x-axis) plot showing a cyclic process with four states. State $p_1, V_1, T_1$ at top left; process 1 (curve, arrow rightward) goes to state $p_2, V_2, T_1$; process 2 (steep curve, arrow downward) goes to state $p_3, V_3, T_2$ at bottom right; process 3 (curve, arrow leftward) goes to state $p_4, V_4, T_2$; process 4 (steep curve, arrow upward) returns to $p_1, V_1, T_1$. Note in box: 'Processes 2 and 4 are adiabatic'. Processes 1 and 3 are isothermal at $T_1$ and $T_2$.

solution.key_concept: For a reversible ideal-gas Carnot cycle, isothermal work is $w = -nRT\ln\frac{V_f}{V_i}$ and adiabatic work is $w = \Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$, with the IUPAC sign convention (work done on the system is positive).
steps: Read the figure: processes 1 ($T_1$, $V_1 \to V_2$) and 3 ($T_2$, $V_3 \to V_4$) are isothermal. Processes 2 ($T_1 \to T_2$) and 4 ($T_2 \to T_1$) are adiabatic. Here $n = 1$ and $R = 2\ \text{cal K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$.
Process 1 (reversible isothermal): $w_1 = -nRT_1\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1} = -2T_1\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$.
Process 3 (reversible isothermal): $w_3 = -2T_2\ln\frac{V_4}{V_3}$. Adding gives $w_1 + w_3 = -2T_1\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1} - 2T_2\ln\frac{V_4}{V_3}$, which matches option (1).

Adiabatic steps ($q = 0$): $w_2 = \Delta U_2 = C_V(T_2 - T_1)$ and $w_4 = \Delta U_4 = C_V(T_1 - T_2)$. So $w_2 + w_4 = \Delta U_2 + \Delta U_4 = 0$. Option (2) needs $\Delta U_2 - \Delta U_4 = 2C_V(T_2 - T_1) \neq 0$, so it is false.
Process 1 + 2: $w_1 + w_2 = -2T_1\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1} + C_V(T_2 - T_1)$. Option (3) has the wrong sign and drops the adiabatic term, so it is false.
Whole cycle: $\Delta U = 0$, so $w_{net} = -q_{net}$. The net work equals minus the enclosed area, which is non-zero. Hence $w_1 + w_2 + w_3 + w_4 \neq 0$, and option (4) is false.
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) should read $\Delta U_2 + \Delta U_4$, which equals zero. Option (3) has the wrong sign and ignores $w_2$. Option (4) fails because the cycle encloses a non-zero area, so net work is not zero even though $\Delta U_{cycle} = 0$.
solution.common_trap: Students confuse $\Delta U_{cycle} = 0$ with $w_{cycle} = 0$, or use $w = +nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$ (the physics sign convention) for expansion work.
solution.time_saving_tip: Write $w_{iso} = -nRT\ln\frac{V_f}{V_i}$ with $nR = 2$ and compare it directly with option (1). The sign and form match at once.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Ionization enthalpy
questions.question: Given below are two statements : One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

statements.A: The first ionization enthalpy of O is lower than that of N and F.
statements.R: The loss of an electron from O leads to stable half-filled $p$ orbital.

options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are correct and R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is correct but R is not correct.
A is not correct but R is correct.

solution.key_concept: Oxygen ($2p^4$) has a lower first ionization enthalpy than nitrogen because removing one electron leaves the stable half-filled $2p^3$ configuration and relieves pairing repulsion. Fluorine is higher than oxygen simply because its nuclear charge is larger.
steps: Write the valence configurations: N $= 2s^2 2p^3$ (half-filled), O $= 2s^2 2p^4$ (one $2p$ orbital doubly occupied), F $= 2s^2 2p^5$.

Recall the approximate values of $\Delta_i H_1$: N $\approx 1402$, O $\approx 1314$, F $\approx 1681\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. So $\Delta_i H_1(\text{O}) < \Delta_i H_1(\text{N})$ and $\Delta_i H_1(\text{O}) < \Delta_i H_1(\text{F})$, and Assertion A is correct.

Ionizing O gives $\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}^+ + e^-$, with $\text{O}^+ = 2s^2 2p^3$. This is an exactly half-filled $p$ subshell, which is extra stable because of symmetry and exchange energy. Reason R is correct.

Losing an electron from O is easier because the electron removed is the paired one, which feels interelectronic repulsion. Its removal produces the stable $2p^3$ arrangement, so less energy is needed. This is why O falls below N, which breaks the general left-to-right increase.
Oxygen is also below fluorine because F has a higher nuclear charge across the period. The NTA key treats R as the correct explanation of the anomalous dip at O.
The key's verdict is that both A and R are correct and R explains A, which matches Option (1).
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) fails because the half-filled $\text{O}^+$ ($2p^3$) configuration is the accepted reason for the dip in ionization enthalpy at O. Options (3) and (4) fail because both A and R are factually true.
solution.common_trap: Students often assume ionization enthalpy rises steadily from N to O to F and mark A false, forgetting the N > O anomaly caused by the half-filled $2p^3$ stability of N and $\text{O}^+$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Memorise the second-period anomalies directly: Be > B and N > O. The cause is always a stable filled or half-filled subshell, either in the parent atom or in the ion formed.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Ideal and non-ideal solutions
questions.question: Consider the following statements about the solutions formed by mixing two liquids.

statements.A: An ideal solution thus formed obeys Raoult's law throughout the composition range.
statements.B: Mixture of chloroform and acetone shows negative deviation from Raoult's law.
statements.C: Mixture of aniline and phenol shows positive deviation from Raoult's law.

solution.key_concept: An ideal solution obeys Raoult's law at all compositions. When the A–B interactions are stronger than the A–A and B–B interactions (for example, through hydrogen bonding), the solution shows negative deviation; when they are weaker, it shows positive deviation.
steps: Statement A: By definition, an ideal solution obeys Raoult's law, $p_i = x_i p_i^0$, over the entire range of composition. It also has $\Delta_{mix}H = 0$ and $\Delta_{mix}V = 0$. So A is correct.

Statement B: In the chloroform–acetone mixture, the H atom of $CHCl_3$ forms a hydrogen bond with the carbonyl O of acetone: $Cl_3C{-}H\cdots O{=}C(CH_3)_2$. The new A–B attractions are stronger than the original A–A and B–B interactions.
Stronger A–B attraction lowers the escaping tendency of the molecules, so $p_{total} < x_A p_A^0 + x_B p_B^0$. This is negative deviation, with $\Delta_{mix}H < 0$, so B is correct.

Statement C: In the aniline–phenol mixture, the acidic O–H of phenol forms a strong hydrogen bond with the basic N of aniline: $C_6H_5O{-}H\cdots NH_2C_6H_5$. These A–B attractions are stronger than the original interactions in either pure liquid.
The vapour pressure is therefore lower than predicted by Raoult's law. The mixture shows negative deviation, not positive, so C is incorrect.
Only A and B are correct, which corresponds to option (1).
solution.why_not_others: Options (2) and (4) both include C, but phenol–aniline shows negative deviation because of strong hydrogen bonding. Option (3) leaves out B, which is a standard textbook example of negative deviation.
solution.common_trap: Students often assume that mixing two hydrogen-bonded liquids always breaks hydrogen bonds and causes positive deviation, as in ethanol–water. They miss that acidic phenol and basic aniline form even stronger A–B hydrogen bonds, which gives negative deviation.
solution.time_saving_tip: Memorise the standard pairs. Chloroform–acetone, phenol–aniline and $HNO_3$–water show negative deviation. Ethanol–acetone, $CS_2$–acetone and ethanol–water show positive deviation. Once you spot that C is false, options (2) and (4) are out, and B being true settles option (1).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: General methods of preparation, properties and reactions
questions.question: One of the products formed in the following reaction is
options: Dicyclohexylamine: two cyclohexane rings connected through an NH group
Bicyclohexyl bearing an $NH_2$ group: a cyclohexane ring attached to another cyclohexane ring, with $NH_2$ on the carbon adjacent to the ring junction (2-cyclohexylcyclohexylamine)
Bicyclohexyl: two cyclohexane rings directly bonded to each other
questions.diagram_description: Reaction: cyclohexylmagnesium bromide (cyclohexane ring–MgBr) + cyclohexylamine (cyclohexane ring–$NH_2$) → ?

solution.key_concept: Grignard reagents are strong bases, so any compound with an acidic hydrogen (on O, N or S, or a terminal alkyne C–H) protonates the carbanion part and gives the corresponding hydrocarbon.
steps: In cyclohexylmagnesium bromide, $C_6H_{11}MgBr$, the C–Mg bond is highly polar. The cyclohexyl carbon behaves as a carbanion ($C_6H_{11}^-$), which is a very strong base.
Cyclohexylamine, $C_6H_{11}NH_2$, has acidic N–H hydrogens (p$K_a \approx 35$). These are far more acidic than the C–H of cyclohexane (p$K_a \approx 50$).
An acid–base reaction therefore occurs before any substitution can happen: $C_6H_{11}MgBr + C_6H_{11}NH_2 \rightarrow C_6H_{12} + C_6H_{11}NHMgBr$.
The carbanion picks up $H^+$ from N and becomes cyclohexane, $C_6H_{12}$. The amine is converted into a magnesium amide salt.
Of the products formed, only cyclohexane appears among the options.
solution.why_not_others: The $NH_2$ group is a very poor leaving group, so the Grignard reagent cannot displace it to form a C–C bond (bicyclohexyl) or a C–N bond (dicyclohexylamine). It also cannot substitute on a ring C–H to give the $NH_2$-bearing bicyclohexyl. Simple deprotonation of the N–H is the only reaction that takes place.
solution.common_trap: Treating the Grignard reagent as a nucleophile that couples with the amine, giving dicyclohexylamine or bicyclohexyl, instead of recognising the fast acid–base reaction with the N–H hydrogen.
solution.time_saving_tip: Whenever RMgX meets a compound containing O–H, N–H, S–H or a terminal $\equiv C$–H, write R–H straight away; here R–H is cyclohexane.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Unique behaviour of the first element in each group
questions.question: The correct statement is
options: Boron has a maximum covalency of four.
Magnesium has a maximum covalency of four.

solution.key_concept: Second-period elements have only four valence orbitals ($ns$ and three $np$, no $d$ orbitals), so their maximum covalency is four, whereas third-period elements can use vacant $3d$ orbitals and exceed four.
steps: Count the valence orbitals. Period-2 elements (Be, B) have $2s + 2p_x + 2p_y + 2p_z$ = 4 valence orbitals and no $2d$ subshell. Period-3 elements (Mg, Al) have $3s$, three $3p$ and five $3d$ orbitals = 9 valence orbitals.
Statement (1): Boron has only 4 valence orbitals, so its maximum covalency is 4, as in $[BF_4]^-$ and $[B(OH)_4]^-$. This is correct.
Statement (2): Beryllium is also in period 2, so it has 4 valence orbitals ($2s$ + three $2p$), not 3. This is incorrect.
Statement (3): Magnesium is in period 3 and can use vacant $3d$ orbitals, so its maximum covalency is greater than 4, i.e. 6 (e.g. $[Mg(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$). This is incorrect.
Statement (4): Aluminium has $3s$, $3p$ and $3d$ orbitals available, giving 9 valence orbitals, not 5. It shows covalency up to 6, as in $[AlF_6]^{3-}$. This is incorrect.
Only statement (1) is correct, which matches the official answer.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Boron has a maximum covalency of four.
solution.why_not_others: Be has four valence orbitals, not three. Mg and Al, being period-3 elements with vacant $3d$ orbitals, can show covalency up to six (e.g. $[AlF_6]^{3-}$), and Al has nine valence orbitals, not five.
solution.common_trap: Students count only the occupied orbitals (e.g. Be's $2s^2$, or Al's $3s^23p^1$) instead of all available valence orbitals, or they assume Mg, like Be, is limited to a covalency of four.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember the rule: period 2 means exactly 4 valence orbitals and a maximum covalency of 4, while period 3 has $d$ orbitals and a covalency of up to 6. Option (1) is the only one fitting this rule.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Entropy of the universe and Gibbs energy as criteria for spontaneity
questions.question: A protein undergoes reversible thermal denaturation from its initial state N to denatured state D according to $N \rightleftharpoons D$. At $60^\circ C$, the concentrations of both N and D are equal at equilibrium, and the standard enthalpy change of denaturation of $666\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$. The standard entropy change ($\Delta S^\circ$ in $kJ\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$) of the protein upon denaturation at $60^\circ C$ is closest to:

solution.key_concept: At equilibrium with $K = 1$, $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = 0$, so $\Delta H^\circ = T\Delta S^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ = \dfrac{\Delta H^\circ}{T}$ (with $T$ in kelvin).
steps: For $N \rightleftharpoons D$, $[N] = [D]$ at equilibrium, so $K = \dfrac{[D]}{[N]} = 1$.
Then $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -RT\ln 1 = 0$.
From $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = 0$, we get $\Delta S^\circ = \dfrac{\Delta H^\circ}{T}$.
Convert the temperature to kelvin: $T = 60 + 273 = 333\ K$.
Substitute: $\Delta S^\circ = \dfrac{666\ kJ\ mol^{-1}}{333\ K} = 2.0\ kJ\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (4), $11.1$, comes from dividing by $60$ (Celsius) instead of $333\ K$. Option (2), $2000$, is the correct value in $J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$ but the question asks for $kJ$. Option (3), $333$, is just the temperature in kelvin.
solution.common_trap: Using the temperature in °C ($60$) instead of kelvin ($333\ K$), or reporting the answer in $J$ when $kJ$ is asked.
solution.time_saving_tip: Equal concentrations at equilibrium means $K = 1$ and $\Delta G^\circ = 0$, so directly compute $\Delta S^\circ = \Delta H^\circ / T = 666/333 = 2$.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: VSEPR theory and shapes of simple molecules
questions.question: Match the species in List I with their geometry in List II. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.key_concept: The shape of a species follows from its electron pairs around the central atom (VSEPR, $sp^3$, $sp^3d$, $sp^3d^2$), while for a complex like $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ it follows from the hybridisation set by the strong-field ligand ($dsp^2$).
steps: A. $PCl_5$: P has 5 valence electrons and forms 5 P–Cl bonds with 0 lone pairs. That is 5 bond pairs, $sp^3d$ hybridisation, so the shape is trigonal bipyramidal (III).

B. $BrF_5$: Br has 7 valence electrons. Five go into Br–F bonds, leaving 1 lone pair. That is 6 electron pairs (5 bp + 1 lp), $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation. The electron geometry is octahedral, and with one position taken by the lone pair the shape is square pyramidal (IV).
C. $BF_4^-$: B has 3 valence electrons, plus 1 from the negative charge, giving 4. These form 4 B–F bonds with 0 lone pairs, $sp^3$ hybridisation, so the shape is tetrahedral (I).

D. $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$: Ni is in the $+2$ state, which is $3d^8$. $CN^-$ is a strong-field ligand, so the 8 d-electrons pair up in four 3d orbitals and leave one 3d orbital empty. Hybridisation is $dsp^2$, so the shape is square planar (II), and the complex is diamagnetic.
Matching: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II, which is option (2).
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) gives $PCl_5$ a square pyramidal shape, but it has no lone pair, so it must be trigonal bipyramidal. Options (3) and (4) make $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ square pyramidal, which is impossible for a 4-coordinate species; (3) also wrongly makes $BrF_5$ tetrahedral and $BF_4^-$ square planar, and (4) wrongly makes $BrF_5$ square planar.
solution.common_trap: Students often apply a simple 4-pairs-means-tetrahedral rule to $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ and forget that strong-field $CN^-$ forces $dsp^2$ (square planar), unlike $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$, which is $sp^3$ and tetrahedral.
solution.time_saving_tip: Fix the two sure matches first: $PCl_5$ is trigonal bipyramidal (III), which eliminates option (1), and $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ is square planar (II), which eliminates (3) and (4). Only option (2) remains.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Mechanism of electrophilic addition: hydrogen, halogens, water and hydrogen halides
questions.question: Given below are two statements: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.

statements.I: trans-But-2-ene upon treatment with $Br_2$ in $CCl_4$ gives the following product [Newman projection]
statements.II: cis-But-2-ene upon treatment with alkaline $KMnO_4$ gives the following product. [Newman projection]

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.diagram_description: Statement I Newman projection: front carbon has Br (top), H (lower left), Me (lower right); back carbon has Br (bottom), H (upper left), Me (upper right). Statement II Newman projection: front carbon has OH (top), H (lower left), Me (lower right); back carbon has Me (bottom), H (upper left), OH (upper right).

solution.key_concept: $Br_2$ adds anti and alkaline $KMnO_4$ adds syn, so the trans- and cis-but-2-enes give products whose meso or racemic nature can be read from the Newman projection.
steps: Expected products: anti addition of $Br_2$ to trans-but-2-ene gives meso-2,3-dibromobutane. Syn dihydroxylation of cis-but-2-ene by cold alkaline $KMnO_4$ gives meso-butane-2,3-diol.

Test for meso in a Newman projection: in the staggered conformation where like groups are anti, the meso form has $Br/Br$ (or $OH/OH$), $Me/Me$ and $H/H$ each anti. That conformation has a centre of symmetry.

Statement I: Br is at $0^\circ$ (front) and $180^\circ$ (back), so the Br atoms are anti. The front Me is at $120^\circ$ and the back Me at $60^\circ$, which is gauche, not anti. Likewise the H atoms at $240^\circ$ and $300^\circ$ are gauche.
So the Statement I structure has no centre of symmetry. It is one enantiomer of the chiral $(\pm)$ dibromide, which comes from cis-but-2-ene, not the meso product. Statement I is incorrect.

Statement II: the front carbon has OH at $0^\circ$, Me at $120^\circ$ and H at $240^\circ$. Rotate the back carbon by $120^\circ$ so that its OH sits at $180^\circ$. Its Me then sits at $300^\circ$ and its H at $60^\circ$.
Now $OH/OH$, $Me/Me$ ($120^\circ$ vs $300^\circ$) and $H/H$ ($240^\circ$ vs $60^\circ$) are all anti. A centre of symmetry exists, so this is meso-butane-2,3-diol. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: The figure for Statement I shows anti Br atoms, so it looks like anti addition, but its Me groups are gauche. That makes it the chiral (racemic) dibromide rather than the meso product, so options (1) and (3) fail. Statement II correctly shows the meso diol, so option (2) fails.
